## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

and each is built on the public facts named here.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

screens.why1: Opening the buying-decision part with the idea itself is the obvious start, since everything I'm asked next about buying it depends on knowing what it is.

screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.

screens.instead: Imagine Codyco, an AI reservation agent that picks up the booking calls nobody answers. When no one at your reservations office takes a call, it is forwarded to Codyco. It answers guests' questions the way your hotel would, takes the payment and puts the confirmed booking straight into your PMS. Calls go to your agents by rules you set. The people building it believe it would turn the calls you miss into bookings.

screens.why3: I know my own approval limit and when a property owner has to agree, so I answer this from what I do every budget round.
screens.why4: The four run cleanly from me alone, to the owner, to a committee, to not my call at all, and I can't say fits as the way out.
screens.why5: It names an owner, a role I recognise from managed and owned hotels, and nothing of the product's pitch reaches me.
screens.why6: One short either-or question, then four short options and the one escape; easy to hold by ear.
screens.why7: The four fixed answers run in order from alone to someone else's call, the tested role (the hotel's owner) sits in the second, and I can't say stands apart, so both for and against are possible.

screens.why1: After who signs off, the next thing I would think about is what has to clear before we can switch on an AI answering our guest calls, so this fits here.
screens.why2: A Datenschutz review of guest calls is something every German hotel group knows, and I would understand the question on first hearing.
screens.why3: I have taken call recording and new booking tools past our data protection officer before, so I can put a realistic time on it.
screens.why4: The bands are clean and do not overlap, it wouldn't be needed is a real answer, and I can't tell is the right way out.
screens.why5: Only the name Codyco from the idea card comes through, and the step is in my own words, with nothing of the founder's pitch leaking.
screens.why6: Said in two steps, four options and then a two-way follow-up, it is easy to hold and answer by ear.
screens.why7: There is one measure, the step's own time, with five bands around the edge at 4 weeks plus not needed, a German buyer-side brake as the step, both sides possible, and I can't tell as the only escape.

screens.why1: Right after I said the data protection review would take 4 weeks to 3 months, it makes sense to ask what drags it out.
screens.why2: The words are plain, but 'You said 4 weeks to 3 months' doesn't say for what, and 'in buying Codyco' widens it from the data protection review I was asked about, so I'd have to work out whether they mean the review or the whole purchase.
screens.why3: I know exactly what slows this down for us: our data protection officer, the works council if calls are recorded, the processing agreement with the vendor, and the owners' sign-off.
screens.why4: A free-text box, no options.
screens.why5: Codyco was introduced on the idea card, and nothing new about the product or the founder's terms reaches me here.
screens.why6: Two short sentences, one question, easy to hear once and answer.
screens.instead: You said the data protection review would take 4 weeks to 3 months. What would make it take that long?

screens.why1: After price, who pays, who signs off and the data protection review, the obvious last question is whether I would actually put money into a first hotel.
screens.why2: A paid pilot at one hotel with money back is how we trial any booking or call tool in our group, so I read it once and know what I am agreeing to.
screens.why3: I decide on and pay for these tools myself, so whether I would fund a €3,000 pilot at one house is my own call.
screens.why4: Four distinct answers from firm yes to firm no, and the soft yes (a demo on sample calls first) is exactly what I would ask for before signing anything.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's terms (€3,000, money-back, one hotel, Codyco named on the card) and nothing reads like their internal language.
screens.why6: One short question; the first option is long but it is just the question repeated as a yes, and the other three are short enough to hold by ear, with €3,000 saying cleanly as three thousand euros.
screens.why7: The first yes takes the founder's own paid step whole, the soft yes names a free smaller step because the pilot costs money, two answers are for and two against, and there is no escape, as the card requires.
